ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Allocation under SGRY to Gujarat 
*461. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENTbe pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have any scheme to launch Sampoma 
Grameen RozgarYojna; 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) the funds allocated/proposed to be allocated to the State of Gujarat 
under the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PAITL): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Government launched the Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojna 
(SGRY) 
on 25th September, 2001 and the Scheme is in operation throughout the 
country. 
(b) The Sampooma Grameen Rozgar  Yojna (SGRY) was launched to 
provide additional wage employment and food security to the rural poor 
through 
creation of need-based infrastructure in  the rural areas. The Scheme is being 
implemented through the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). The funds and 
1 

RAJYA SABHA            [23 April, 2003] 
foodgrains are distributed among the District Panchayats, Intermediate Level 
Panchayats and Gram Panchayats in the ratio of 20:30:50. The wages are paid 
to the workers partly in foodgrains and partly in cash. However, a minimum 
25% of the wages is required to be paid in cash. 
(c) During the current year (2003-2004), an amount of Rs. 89.66 crores 
alongwith 96725 MTs of foodgrains has been allocated under the Sampooma 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana (Stream-I and Stream-II) to the State Government of 
Gujarat

[23 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THEMINISTEROF STATEINTHEMMSTRYOFPERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Approach Paperto the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—
2007) focuses on governance as a critical factor for promotion of economic 
development The formulation of viable schemes for bringing about 
development especially in the social sector and an appropriate delivery 
system to implement such schemes have been identified for the above 
purpose and good governance has been identified as intrinsic to both. 
Transparency in governmental functioning, greater accountability across all 
the sectors of government, use of information technology so as to reduce 
discretion and delay, security of tenure, tackling corruption and strengthening 
the rule of law, promotion of gender equality have been, inter-alia, the 
governance reforms suggested.

constituted on 19 February, 2003 to formulate specific changes in the systems 
and procedures, in consultation with Ministries/Departments concerned, and 
to devise strategies for changing attitudes. The Group is required to prepare 
an Action Plan for implementation of its recommendations within a time-

constituted on 20 February, 2003. 
3. The first meeting of the Core Group on Administrative Reforms 
(CGAR) was held on 3 March, 2003, in which the following eight subjects 
were identified for preparing Concept Papers along with Action Plans: 
(i) How to make the administration efficient and transparent? 
(ii) How to make the administration responsive and citizen-friendly? 
(iii) How to make the administration accountable? 
(iv) Simplification of rules, regulations and procedures and creating 
public awareness about them; 
(v) Delegation of authority from 'nodal' Ministries, to 'functional' 
Ministries, within the Ministries and from the Ministries to their 
field offices;

Package for SEBs 
 *476.    SHRI GAYA SINGH :††                   
SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that Govern ment have allocated Rs. 40,000 
crore as package to reform the State Electricity Boards; and 
(b) if so, the details of the package and steps proposed to be taken to 
reduce the losses of the Boards? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM 
GEETE): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Government has approved the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) during the 10th Plan period 
for upgradation of distribution system covering densely electrified zones 
focusing on urban and industrial areas. The proposed outlay is Rs. 40.000 
crores, comprising of Rs. 20,000 crores towards investment component and 
another Rs. 20,000 crores towards the incentive component. The funding 
through budgetary support on a yearly basis would be based on need, 
utilization and availability of funds. The Programme aims at reducing the 
cash losses to improve financial viability of the State Electricity Boards 
(SEBs)/ Utilities. The programme has tw o components, namely investment 
component and incentive component to encourage/motivate utilities to reduce 
cash losses. Under the investment scheme, APDRP will finance specific 
projects 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Gaya 
Singh. 
30 

   [23 April, 2003]                RAJYASABHA 
relating to upgradation and strengthening of subtransmission & distribution 
network including, inter alia, energy accounting & metering. The incentive 
scheme aims at actual cash loss reduction by SEBs/Utilities. Under this 
scheme, grant amounting to fifty per cent of the actual cash loss reduction 
effected by SEB/Utility would be provided. 
Under the Memorandum of Agreement signed between the SEBs and 
the Ministry of Power, the SEBs have agreed for taking steps to reduce the 
losses and to reduce outages and interruptions and thus reduce Aggregate 
Technical & Commercial losses. These steps, inter-alia, include metering of 
11 KV feeders and all consumers; un dertake energy audit at all levels; 
upgrading and stengthening of distribution system; introduction of 
Information Technology for automation, billing & collection of revenue, etc.

Important measure taken to prevent, out-break of fire are listed 
below.— 
In underground mines: 
(i) Extraction of coal by forming panels of proper size which can be 
extracted within the incubation period. 
(ii) Constructing preparatory stoppings to enable quick isolation of 
the panel in case of out-break of fire. 
(iii) Monitoring environmental conditions in extraction areas, sealed 
off areas, old workings, return airways for early detection of 
fires. 
(iv) Blanketing of surface areas over extracted areas. 
(v) Inspection of workings, isolation/fire-stoppings, including old 
workings on idle days. 
(vi) Environmental tele-monitoring systems are being installed in a 
phased manner in some fiery and highly gassy underground 
mines. Already thirteen such sy stems are in operation and two 
more such systems are under procurement. 
In opencast mines: 
(i) Blanketing of exposed benches in coal seams prone to 
spontaneous heating and in coal stocks. 
(ii) Provision for waler-spraying. 
(iii) Regular inspection of coal dumps, OB dumps, stocks etc.

Judicious exploitation of mineral resources 
3492. SHRI R. P. GOE NKA : Will the Minister of MINES be pleased 
to State: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a recent report 
entitled "undermining Inc ia" brought out by Kalpvariksh, a Non-
Governmental Organisation highligthing that indiscriminate mining of 
bauxite, iron ore, lime stone etc. in certains parts of the country is destroying 
some of the most ecologically sensitive areas, including catchment mat 
provide water to millions of people, and is a threat to long term water 
security; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) details of fresh strategies drawn up for a more judicious exploitation 
of the mineral resources of the country ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESHBAIS): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Mines, Government of India is 
aware of recent Newspaper reports on the concerns expressed in a study done 
by Kalpavariksh, a non-Governmenta l Organisation, in their report 
"Undermining India". 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993 (NMP), inter alia recognizes that 
the policies governing the mining and mineral sector should be harmonized 
with the policies governing industrial and socio-economic developments in 
the country. Some mineral rich areas are ecologically fragile and some are 
biologically rich. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA                     [23 April, 2003] 
NMP states that it is necessary to take comprehensive view to facilitate the 
choice or order of land use keeping in view the needs of development as well 
as needs of protecting the forests, environment and ecology. Both aspects 
have to be properly coordinated to  facilitate and ensure a sustainable 
development of mineral resources in harmony with environment. 
As envisaged in the NMP, in order to ensure scientific and systematic 
mining with due regard to environment, under mining statutes, no mining 
lease can be granted without an approved mining plan. Stringent penalties 
have been provided for violations of Mineral Conservation and Development 
Rules, 1988. Mining activities are also subject to other laws of the land 
including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980 and rules made thereunder. Mi ning industry is also required to 
follow the air pollution and water pollution norms. For major mining projects 
of bauxite, iron ore, limestone etc., public hearing and environmental impact 
assessment studies are required before mining leases are granted. In addition, 
mining in ecologically fragile regions is restricted under specific Regulations 
and Notifications like the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, Aravalli 
Notification, etc. 
The independent studies and reports on effect of mining on environment 
brought out from time to time help the Government in taking policy decisions 
and streamlining the monitoring mechanism for sustainable development of 
mineral resources in harmony with environment, which is an ongoing 
process.

3495. PROF. R. B. S. VARMA: Will the Minister of PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS be pleased to state:

can review its final allocation orders in case of the division of any State in the

Court;  
(c) if not, the reasons therefor;

allocation orders, on receipt of the r ecommendations of the State Advisory

regards SERCs, States have been given flexibility in regard to setting up of 
Regulatory Commissions as also in terms of conferring certain functions on 
them. Sub-section (1) of section 22 of the Act stipulates mandatory functions 
of SERCs while Sub-section (2) of sec tion 22 provides for optional functions 
which may be conferred upon the

Commissions on some other aspects of regulation as well.

Power to neighbouring states by DPP 
3504. SHRISURESH PACHOURI: W ill the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to State: 
(a) whether Government of Maharashtra is working on revival of 
Dabhol Power Project; 
(b) if so,whether the Central Government has taken any initiative in this 
regard; 
(c)once operationalised, whether there is any proposal to sell surplus 
power to neighbouring State like Madhya Pradesh; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) Government of Maharashtra 
(GOM) has taken a decision to allow th e Maharashtra State Electricity Board 
(MSEB) to draw power from Phase-I (740 MW) of Dabhol Power Project at 
an optimum level of 83% at a tariff of about Rs. 2.80/KWH of an interim 
basis subject to approval of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory 
Commission (MERC) and High Court of Maharashtra which has appointed a 
receiver for the project, and without prejudice to MSEB/GOM's rights and 
contentions in the pending arbitration/ judicial and MERC proceedings. 
(b) The power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in regard to the Dabhol 
Power Project was entered into between MSEB and Dabhol Power Company 
(DPC). Thus, the responsibility to restart Phase-I and complete Phase-II of 
the Dabhol project lies with the main stakeholders viz. MSEB and DPC as 
well as the Government of Maharashtra. The Indian Financial Institutions 
(IFIs) led by the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), having 
substantial stakes in the Dabhol Power Project, have been trying to 
restructure and revive the Dabhol plant. Government of India has agreed to 
facilitate any amicable solution to the various issues in order to revive/ 
restructure the project. Any scheme finalized for revival of the Dabhol 
project would come as a comprehensive package and would have to resolve 
complex, legal, financial and technical issues. While this may take time, as a 
first step, it has been agreed that an interim revival package for restarting 
Phase-I be worked out by the concerned agencies. It has been decided that 
the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) would act as the 
 129 
 

RAJYA SABHA            [23 April, 2003] 
Operation & Maintenance Contractor for running Phase-I. At the instance of 
the Government of India (Ministry of Power), a team involving 
representatives from NTPC, M/s GE I ndia, M/s Bechtel, IDBI, MSEB and 
Central Electricity Authority carried out a preliminary inspection of the 
Dabhol power plant from Oct. 28-30, 2002 to ascertain its condition and to 
work out an action plan for restart of phase-1. 
(c) Under the proposed scheme mentioned above, the power generated 
from Phase-I would be absorbed by MSEB. No decision has been taken and 
conveyed to the Government of India with regard to off-take of power from 
phase-II after it is completed. 
(d) The question of selling of surplus power (if any), from the Dabhol 
power project to neighbouring States like Madhya Pradesh, would be decided 
by the Government of Maharashtra and would depend upon the overall 
restructuring of the Dabhol Plant and related issues such as quantum of off-
take of power by Maharashtra and the final power tariff etc. after completion 
of phase-II.

(b) The Government has approved the Accelearated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for upgradation of 
distribution system covering densely electrified zones focusing on urban and 
industrial areas. The proposed outlay for the programme is Rs. 40,000 crores, 
comprising of Rs. 20,000 crores towards investment component and another 
Rs. 20,000 crores towards the incentive component in the 10th Five Year 
Plan. The actual funding through budget ary support on a yearly basis would 
be based on need, utilization and availability of funds. The Programme aims 
at reducing the cash losses to improve financial viability of the State 
Electricity Boards (SEBs)AJtilities. The programme has two components, 
namely investment component and incentive component to 
encourage/motivate utilities to reduce cash losses. Under the investment 
scheme, APDRP will finance specific projects relating to upgradation and 
strengthening of sub-transmission & distribution network including energy 
accounting & metering in the distributi on circles in a phased manner. The 
incentive scheme aims at actual cash loss reduction by SEBs/Utilities. Under 
this scheme, grant amounting to fifty per cent of the actual cash loss 
reduction effected by SEBs Utilities would be provided. 
(c) All the State Electricity Boards/Utilities in the States are eligible for 
assistance under the Programme. 
(d) The activities taken up under APDRP would result in the following 
measurable outcomes: 
 
> Reduction of AT&C losses from the existing around 50% to 
around 15% in five years to begin with in the urban areas and 
high density/ consumption areas; 
> Significant improvement in revenue realization by reduction 
commercial losses leading to additional realization of an 
additional Rs. 20,000 crores, approximately over a period of 4 
to 5 years; 
> Reduction of technical losses would result in additional energy 
of nearly 6,000—7,000 MW to the system, avoiding the need of 
9,000 to 11,000 MW of fresh capacity additional besides 
avoiding investments to the tune of Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 60,000 
crores; 
> Quality of supply and reliable,  interruption-free power will 
encourage usage of energy e fficient equipments/appliances, 
which will further lead to improvement in availability of energy.

3522. SHRIJANARDHANA POOJAR Y: Will the Minister of

Electricity Boards are in a precariou s position with total transmission and 
distribution (T&D) losses accounting for Rs. 30,000 crores annually; 
(b) if so, the measures initiated by Government to mitigate the situation; 
 
(c) whether it is a fact that the Centre proposes to launch an incentive 
scheme to help States to minimize the T&D losses; and 
(d) if so, the details of the scheme and the States which have so far 
qualified for the incentive?

(SffiUMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) To improve the financial viability of the State Electricity Boards 
(SEBs)/Utilities the Central Government  have launched the Accelerated 
Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP). The Programme has two 
components, namely, investment component and incentive component. Under 
investment component, the Central Government provides assistance to the 
tune 
of 50% ( by way of loan and matching grant) of the project cost for the 
upgradation and modernization of distribution system in high density load 
centres 
like towns and industrial centres in non special cat egory states and 100% 
assistance (by way of 90% grant and 10%  loan) in case of special category 
states.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES

international market it is desirable to utilize all resources optimally and

of

from 
Gherzi Textile Organisation. The main findings of the study include:— 
• India's very low productivity (yield per hectare) results' in higher 
cost of raw cotton. 
• Power cost plays an important role more due to the factor cost, in 
the manufacturing cost of cotton textiles. 
• Inadequate investment across the value chain restricting growth of 
technologically upgraded capacity and the quality of out-put of the 
cotton textile industry, possible due to relative high cost of capital. 
• If the current scenario continues, i ndustry's present market share in 
the global market may shrink and ma y lead to adversely impact the 
domestic market. 
It is for the individual units to explore the possibilities for decreasing 
the cost of production by adopting various measures in order to remain 
competitive in the international market.

SHRI MATI N. P. DURGA  (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, it 
gives me immense pleasure to speak on this Bill which has been brought 
before us to amend sections 2 and 3 of the Prevention of Insults to National 
Honour Act, 1971.1 wholeheartedly welcome the move of the Government. 
Sir, flying the National Flag is governed by the Emblem and Names 
(Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 195 0, and the Prevention of Insults to 
National Honour Act, 1971. And, the Flag code brings together all such laws, 
conventions, practices and instructi ons for guidance and benefit of all 
concerned. As the House is aware, th e National Flag was adopted by the 
constituent Assembly on 22nd Jury, 1947, and all our National Symbols 
National Flag, State Emblem, National Anthem, National Song, National 
Calendar, National Animal, National Bird and National Flower derived their 
sanctity from our constitution. 
We have become independent and have got the pride of having our 
own 
269 

RAJYASABHA [23 April, 2003] 
National Mag after sacrifices made by millions of our people. We are honouring 
the National Flag. But alas! We have given little recognition to a great patriot, 
freedom fighter and architect of our Nati onal Flag. With your permission, I 
would just say a few lines on this. In our country, for the first time, we had 
unfurled our flag on 7th August, 1906, at Green Park in Calcutta. It had got the 
colours of red, yellow and green, with flowers and written on it 'Vande 
Mataram'. With some minor changes, almost similar kind of flag was unfurled in 
1907. In 1917, one more flag was prepared with 7 stars. But, in 1921, the 
Congress came under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and met at 
Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh. There, a young patriot, Shri Pingali Venkaiah, 
prepared our National Flag. He had done a lot of research, by that time, on the 
Indian Flag and had also written a book, called,' India's National Flag'. The 
National Flag was unfurled by the Home Rule Flag Union in Lucknow in 1916. 
But, when a meeting of the Congress took place in March, 1921, at 
Vijayawada, Shri Pingali Venkaiah showed the Flag prepared by him to 
Mahatma Gandhi. Bapu liked this Flag very much, and in 1931, the All India 
Congress Committee adopted this Flag. But, since 1921, this Flag was being 
unfurled, unofficially, in all the Congress and other meetings. The only 
difference between the Flag prepared by Shri Pingali Venkaiah and the present 
Flag is, now we have got the 'Dharma Chakra' in place of 'Ratna'. Sir, Mahatma 
Gandhi also wanted to adopt the Flag as it is, but the problem is that the Flag 
should look identifical from the front side and the backside. And if'Ratna' were 
retained, it would not have looked identica l. This is one of the main reasons for 
replacing 'Ratna' with Dharma Chakra'. Sir, Gandhiji had written appreciatingly 
about Shri Pingali Venkaiah in 'The Young India. ' But, what honour have we 
given to this great patriot? We have not done anything, literally. It pains us a lot 
because the great architect of this Flag  has not got the due recognition that he 
should have got. We have been, persistently, bringing this to the notice of the 
Government of India to honour him, but in vain. So, now, the time has come, 
and I thought that this is t he appropriate occasion to bring this to the notice of 
the Government of India. So, Madam, I request, through y ou, the Government 
of India to release a postal stamp and erect a statue of Shri Pingali Venkaiah in 
the premises of this great democratic in stitution, which, I am sure, would be a 
befitting tribute to this great man a nd freedom fighter who has given us the 
National Flag. 
The next point is: I welcome the inclusion of this explanation which 
makes it further clear as to what all constitutes disrespect to the National Flag. 
But, 
270 

[23 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
does merely providing a law guarantee any respect? I strongly believe that 
legislations or codes will not make much difference unless and until a feeling 
of nationalism and patriotism is inculcat ed and efforts are made to associate 
people themselves with these National Symbols. Now, the National Anthem is 
being made available at various websites and it can be downloaded on mobile 
phones for ringer tones. I strongly oppose this. I oppose this because you 
should not stop the National Anthem abruptly. It is a sheer disrespect to our 
National Anthem. And, if you are using this as a ringer tone, you would stop it 
abruptly to attend your call. So, I strongly urge the hon. Minister to issue 
directions to the people concerned to stop using not only our National 
Anthem. But also our National Song as ringer tones. 
I would like to raise one more issue, that is, about westernisation of our 
culture, and how our people, especially, during cricket and other matches in 
other countries, show disrespect to our National Flag. The people in the West 
use their National Flag as shirts, caps, shorts tattoos, or use as some other 
draper. Our people are copying this and they have started painting their faces 
and bodies with the National Flag, and have started tattooing the National 
Flag on their cheeks, or, are getting the Flags stitched as shirt or trousers. Not 
only other people, but even our cricketers are embossing the National Flag on 
their gloves and pads. Does it not am ount to showing disrespect to the Flag, 
according to this Act? So, I request t he hon. Minister to take steps and stop 
the occurrence of these incidents, especially, in foreign countries. 
Madam, with these words, I whole heartedly support the move of the 
Government and request the hon. Minister to assure this House that the 
Government of India would honour Shri Pingali fenkaiah in a befitting manner 
by releasing a Postal Stamp and erecti ng a statue in the premises of the 
Parliament, immediately. Thank you, Madam.

*SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Madam, Deputy Chairperson, I rise to 
support this Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill on behalf 
of AIADMK. It is said that this amending Bill has been brought because 
incidents of disrespect to national flag and other national symbols had come to 
the notice of the Government. This am endment provides for punishment even 
for showing disrespect to national symbols. The new Section 3-A provides that 
if a person commits such offence second time or time and again, he will be 
given a punishment of at least one-year. But I request the Minister to consider 
giving more punishment to those who commit this offence again and again. 
The Home Ministry should not think that its duty is over by providing 
punishment for those who show disrespect to national symbols. The 
Government should take st eps to inculcate patriotic feelings in the people, 
particularly the youth. The Government should create such an atmosphere so 
that people respect national symbols on  their own. These days we find people 
waving national flags only in the cricket stadiums. This shows that national 
feelings should be inculcated in the yo uth in the way they like. Functions like 
Independence Day and Republic Day are celebrated only in Government 
Offices and schools and colle ges. The general public are not able to be a part 
of such functions. It is the duty of t he Government to see that such functions 
are held in the nooks and corners of the country with the help of NGOs and 
other such organisations. Patriotic f eelings should come on its own. Such 
environment should exist. 
Finally I wish to make one point This House is unanimous in its view that 
all those who show disrespect to the national symbols should be punished. But 
we should realize that we can respect the national symbol only if we protect 
our nation. There is a sayi ng in Tamil. The translation goes thus: We ought to 
have a wall in order to make a drawing. 
But when action is taken against those who want to divide the country, 
there are people who support such separatists. I wish to ask, are they 
patriots? Will it be wTong to punish such people? I request this august House 
to ponder over this. 
Madam, the centre should support the State Governments when action is 
taken against anti-nationals, separatis ts, supporters of terrorists and those 
who have regular contacts with banned organisations. A nation cannot 
progress just by showing respect to national symbols. Stringent action should 
be taken against anti-national forces.

PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM : Sir, from the statement, I understand that 
the Speed Post centres in Tamil Nadu are not adequate. Only 384 centres are 
thefe in 29 districts. Will the Minister consider increasing the number of Speed 
Post centres in all the districts? Moreover, the rates charged by the Postal 
Department are high as compared to the rates charged by private courier 
services. For example, the Postal Department charges Rs. 30 for speed post from 
Kanyakumari to Chennai, which is a distance of 850 Kms., and a private 
courier service charges only Rs. 12/-. Will the Government review these rates 
and compete with the other delivery systems? 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, in Tamil Nadu, there are 384 Post Offices 
which take Speed post. They are distributed all over the State. There are certain 
norms which have to be followed for setting up such centres. For instance, for a 
National Speed Post Centre, the business must be of about Rs. 45,000 per 
month in regard to Speed Post. Similarly, they should be connected by flights to 
the other places so that you can deliver the post on next day of booking, or by 
the second day. Similarly, there are certain norms for se tting up Speed Post 
centres and Extension Counters. Sir, as the business grows, naturally, we would 
want to increase the number of Speed Post centres. 
Secondly, on the question of rates, the difficulty is that the Government is 
bound, for instance, to pay salaries to  a particular scale. A private courier 
service may just pick up anybody, pay anything to him, and charge very little. But 
the hon. Member is completely right that we must compete with them. As the 
volume of business grows, we will certainly try our best to reduce the rates. 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM : Sir, my second supplementary is this. Will 
the Government evolve a new scheme to reduce the rates and make them 
equivalent to those beingcharged by private courier services? The other thing 
is... 
MR. CHAIRMAN : No. I will not allow the third supplementary. 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE : Sir, as I mentioned, the rates differ. But if you 
look at some other private couriers, they charge very high rates, and then give 
very big discounts, up to 70 per cent, for bulk handling. In Government also, 
discount schemes are there and, as the volume grows, we will try to increase 
those discounts also.-

Statement 
(a) to (d) Speed Post is a premium product and is run on commercial

service to a particular place would depend on market requirements, customer 
needs, expected business and connectivity required for maintaining service

The 1991 Census does not list any particular area as backward in the State.

districts as backward from the point of view of industrial backwardness. These 
districts are: Barmer, Chum, Sirohi, Jaisalmer, Alwar, Jodhpur, Bhilwara, Nagaur, 
Udaipur, Jhalawar, Jhunjhunu, Sikar, Tonk, Dungarpur, Banswara, Jalore. 
12 districts were identified as backward by the Government of India for 
purposes of Income Tax benefits in 1997.  These districts are: Barmer, Jalore, 
Jaisalmer, Churu, Banswara, Dungarpur, Dholpur, Sawai Madhopur, Tonk, Nagaur, 
Jhalawar, Sikar. 
All the above mentioned districts have been provided with Speed Post 
facility. 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMAD KHAN (DURRU): Sir, as the speed post

Government of India, will the Government conduct the survey to ascertain

as well as the country pertaining to the delay or nondelivery of speed post? And,

SHRI ARUN SHOURIE : Sir, the hon. Member has rightly said that 
speed post facilities are available in all the backward districts in Rajasthan. Sir, the 
Government does make two checks in the delivery of speed post. 
8 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
One is that there are checks every month on transit points to see as to whether 
the actual transiting from particular points is in accordance with the norms; and 
secondly, checks are made on the points of delivery. The third check is on 
rectification of complaints. In regard to Rajasthan—I am going only by the 
figures, if the hon. Member has any other specific case in mind, I will attend to 
it—in the transit cases, the efficiency which has been reported in the monthly 
survey is 99.12% and the same figure has come up in delivery of speed post at 
the point of delivery. At the point of delivery, one can find out, because it is a 
bar coded item. When.the item is delivered, it is then put on the website. There 
are two websites from which a person who has sent the material can verify whether 
it has reached that point or not. Second question is with regard to complaints.

complaints have been settled. This, as a proportion of total traffic of speed post 
handled in Rajasthan, is 0.19 per cent.

     SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:

thereto?

DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) and (b) The Administrative 
Staff College of India, Hyderabad have in a Study Report suggested measures

1411.51 crore.

(i) Nearly eighty-nine percent of the expenditure is towards

economy measures on the basis of the guidelines issued by Ministry 
of Finance from time to time and generating more r eceipts by giving

services.

Letter sorting system in mail trains 
†3593. SHRIMATI GURCHARAN KAUR : Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) when the letter sorting system in the mail trains was introduced and 
what are the reasons for its discontinuation; 
(b) the benefit derived from it inspite of the fact that a mail bogie still 
remains attached with the mail trains; and 
(c) the arrangements to be made by Government to restart the system in 
public interest? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI SU. 
THIRUNAVUKKARASAR): (a) Letter sorting system in sorting Sections in 
trains was introduced in the year 1863. Sorting sections functioning in trains 
were converted into transit section (dealing with closed bags) in a phased 
manner between 1982 to 1985. The main reasons for abolition of sorting sections 
were shortage of adequate space in runni ng sections to handle increased mail 
traffic; extremely unhealthy work environment due to dust, inadequate lighting 
arrangements, high operational cost and lack of motivation in younger staff for 
deployment in running sections involving everyday travelling. 
(b) The benefits derived from the conversion of shorting sections into transit 
sections were better utilization of space for handling exchange of bags and 
reduction in the operational cost. 
(c) At present, there is no proposal for reintroduction of the system of 
sorting section.

Statement-I

Statement-II 
Report of the High Level Committee on Long Term Grain Policy 
Major Recommendations 
The Chairman of the High Level Committee on Long Term Grain 
Policy, Prof. Abhijit Sen submitted the Final Report of the Committee to 
106 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Shri Sharad Yadav, Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public 
Distribution. The Commi ttee Members included, inter alia, Dr. R. 
Radhakrishna, Director, Indira Gandhi  Institute of Development Research, 
Mumbai, Dr. Madhura Swaminathan, Professor of Economics, ISI Kolkata, Shri 
A. Mohandas Moses, ex-MD, FCI and Dr. S.N. Kaul, Consultant, Department 
of Economic Affairs, New Delhi. 
2. The Committee has made far-reach ing recommendations with regard-
to the policy in the short as well as long run on 
(i) Foodgrains-based welfare schemes; 
(ii) Public Distribution System; 
(iii) Minimum Support Prices and Procurement Policy; 
(iv) Policy on Open Market Sales, Exports and Imports; 
(v) Role of private trade; and 
(vi) FCI. 
Long Run Recommendations 
 (i) Welfare Schemes 
With regard to the welfare scheme s, the Committee has recommended a 
massive foodgrains employment programme, expansion of the existing 
Antyodaya scheme to cover the entire destitute population, Central support for 
moving to a cooked Mid-day Meals scheme for all school-going children and 
strengthening programmes for women and children. 
(ii) PDS 
With regard to the Public Distribution System, the Committee has 
recommended a system of Universal PD S with uniform Central Issue Prices 
for rice and wheat for all consumers in all parts of the country. The 
Committee has also recommended that an additional subsidy meant for poor 
consumers or persons in relatively backward regions should be given in cash 
to States. Other recommendations for streamlining the PDS include the 
setting up of an independent watchdog body, relaxation of restrictions on 
eligibility to be a licensed fair price shop dealer, effective implementation of 
the PDS (Control) Order, 2001 and greater responsibilities to be given to 
Panchayati Raj Institutions. 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
(iii) MSP and Procurement Policy 
With regard to Minimum Supp ort Prices, the Committee has 
recommended that the MSP policy should continue with an immediate 
correction. The Committee has re commended that the Commission for 
Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) should go strictly on the basis of C2 
cost of production (i.e. all costs including the imputed costs of family labour, 
owned capital and rental on land) in more efficient regions. It has also 
recommended that the MSP should have statutory status and the CACP should 
be made an empowered statutory body. 
It has further recommended to take  care of the States which impose 
excessive levies on MSP purchase, the Central Government may announce its 
MSP policy by declaring a procurement price inclusive of a uniform 4% 
allowance, which should be the maximum price payable for MSP purchases. 
At this MSP price, the Central Government should underwrite open-ended 
purchase of FAQ grains to assure growers an adequate return on their cost. 
The Committee has also recommended that FCI's operation should focus 
more on Eastern and Central India than in the past. The Committee has further 
recommended that while the Centre should continue to take primary 
responsibility for procurement, proc urement should also become more 
dispersed. With regard to coarsegrains, the Committee has recommended that 
MSP operations should be decentralized  to State Governments with full 
financial support from the Centre. 
Another major recommendation of the Committee is that all compulsory 
levy orders on rice millers under the Essential Commodities Act should be 
removed with immediate effect and be replaced by orders requiring mills to 
custom mill the paddy procured under MSP and give delivery of the resultant 
rice to the Central Pool. 
To ensure improvement in quality, the Committee has recommended that 
Fair Average Quality (FAQ) norms shoul d be adhered to strictly in all 
purchases of grains. In unforeseen ci rcumstances if below FAQ norms grains 
are procured, they should not be taken to the Central Pool and should be 
disposed of at commercial terms. 
Along with the correct MSP policy, the Committee has recommended that 
the Central Government should explore expeditiously with the Insurance 
sector the commercial viability of insurance, devised strictly 
108 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
on actuarial principles, against shortfalls not only of yield but also of prices 
from their past averages computed on an area basis. Any startup subsidy 
required for this should be phased ou t within two years of implementations 
for all except poor and marginal farmers. 
The Committee has also recommended measures for crop diversification 
given the changing dietary patterns. 
(iv) Open market sales, export and imports 
With regard to open market sales, the Committee has recommended that the 
prices should be based on the corresponding Central Issue Prices plus the full 
cost of transport and storage as well as market conditions. 
With regard to export and imports of foodgrains, the Committee has 
recommended that it should be based on the system of variable tariffs and the 
exports should be entirely on private account. 
(v) Role of private trade 
The Committee has recommended that barriers to private trade should be 
eased. The Essential Commodities Act should in normal circumstances apply 
only to situations of natural disasters or other contingencies. However, it has 
recommended that a new set of orders, on the lines of PDS (Control) Order, 
2001 may be required to apply to those who voluntarily enter activities 
encompassed in public procurement and distribution. 
(vi) FCI 
With regard to the Food Corporation of India, the Committee has 
expressed the opinion that it has performed its role reasonably well ' and 
should continue to do so. It has recommended that FCI should move into areas 
where reports of distress sale continue to be received and in such areas FCI 
should open procurement centres. It ha s further recommended that FCI should 
change the way it does business to enable fast commercial oriented decision-
making. It has recommended that the FCI should develop a work culture of total 
quality management. The Committee has recommended that the FCI's role should 
be confined to procurement of major cereals for the PDS, i.e. rice and wheat 
and price support operations in coarse cereals should be handled by State 
agencies. 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
The Committee has suggested that the FCI should identify areas of cost 
control by normating of FCI's costs based on the norms recommended by the 
BICRThe Committee has also suggested several measures to cut down the 
storage and transit losses. 
Short Run Recommendations 
For the immediate short run, the Committee has recommended lowering 
of the MSP to average C2 co st, steps to be taken to give statutory status to 
MSP, removal of levy orders on rice millers and strict maintenance of quality 
specifications. Lowering of the C2 cost has been recommended along with a 
compensation package to be given to State Governments for compensating its 
cultivators, estimated at a total of Rs. 3915 crores. 
The Committee has recommended that the State Governments should be 
free to offer this compensation to farmers in any one or combination of the 
following: 
(i)  Direct per hectare transfer to farmers, 
(ii) Subsidising premiums on insurance schemes on crop incomes/ yield, 
(iii) Specific crop diversification schemes, and 
(iv) Other credit/input linked schemes to offset cost, including 
electricity. 
The other recommendations for the short run, including shifting of the FCI's 
focus to East and Central India and removal of existing bottlenecks in the 
decentralized procurement system. 
The Committee has recommended several stock reduction measures, including 
disposal of old and relaxed quality stocks. It has recommended that the lustre 
lost stocks of wheat should be liquidated by March 31, 2003 and all possible 
steps should be taken to segregate available stocks by age and quality. 
It has further recommended that the FCI implements the method of 
physical verification within a period of three months, keeping in view the 
new sampling method proposed by the ISI. 
With regard to exports, the Committee has recommended that steps should 
be taken to prevent leakages into the domestic market and a 
110 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
review of the current export drive should be taken up as and when stocks 
come down to 35 million tonnes. 
With regard to the PDS, the Committ ee has endorsed an immediate shift 
to a unified PDS, which in its view, would bring back many of the poor and 
moderately poor who have been excluded from the BPL category. The 
unified system should be accompanied by a uniform CIP for all consumers at 
Rs. 4.50 per kg of wheat and Rs. 6 per kg of rice to be accompanied by a 
transfer of 35 paisa per kg of grai n offtake as cash incentive to State 
Governments, conditional on lifting a nd accounting. This should be till 
stocks reduce sufficiently, after which the CIP should be increased towards 
acquisition cost. 
The Committee has furt her recommended that the allocation under 
present Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojna scheme should be doubled and the 
expansion of the Antyodaya Anna Yojana be initiated.

Export of foodgrains 
3621. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have plan to export wheat and rice from its 
bulging Central pool during the year 2003-04; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the rates and the name of the countries to which it has been exported 
or proposed to be exported? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Wheat and Rice are being made available from 
the Central Pool for purposes of exports. 
(c) Foodgrains are offered from the Central pool at the Open Market 
Sale Schemes (Domestic) prices. Howe ver, post-delivery and other WTO 
compatible expenses are allowed to exports. Indian foodgrains, so lifted from 
the Central Pool, are being exported to over 30 countries, mainly located in 
South East and South Asia, Middle East and Africa.

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
Quality of rice under food for work programme 
3623. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
G 
(a) whether rice supplied under the 'Food for Work Programme' to the 
State Governments, is of poor quality; and 
(b) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to supply good 
quality rice to the States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) The following steps have been taken by the Government to ensure 
that only good quality foodgrains including rice are supplied to the States:- 
(i) Ample opportunities are provided to the officials of the State 
Governments/UT Administrations to inspect the stocks prior to 
lifting from the Food Corporation of India (FCI) godowns. 
(ii) Instructions have been issued to all the State Governments/ UT 
Administrations that an officer not below the rank of Inspector 
should be deputed to check the quality of foodgrains before lifting 
from the FCI godowns. 
(iii) The samples of foodgrains are to be jointly drawn and sealed by the 
officers of the State Governments/UT Administrations and the FCI 
from the stocks for display at the counters of Fair Price Shops 
(FPSs) for the benefit of consumers. 
(iv) The officers of the State Governments' and the Ministry pay 
surprise checks of the FPSs, to over see the quality of foodgrains 
being distributed through TPDS. 
(v) The officers of the Department designated as 'Area Officers' for 
monitoring the TPDS work in the respective States also undertake 
visits to the storage depots and the FPSs, during their visit to the 
States to check the quality of foodgrains being issued. 
122

Standardisation of bottled water 
3624. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal with Government to insist on ISI or 
any other standardization for bottled water; 
(b) if so, the nature of standards prescribed for the purpose; and 
(c) the agency to check its compliance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. 
SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide 
their Gazette Notifications No. GSR 75 9 (E) and GSR 760(E) have already 
brought Packaged Drinking Water and Packaged Natural Mineral Water 
under the Mandatory Certification Scheme of the Bureau of Indian 
Standards. 
(b) The Nature of the standards prescr ibed are as per the specifications 
outlined in the IS 14543:1998 for Packaged Drinking Water and 
IS: 13428:1998 for Natural Packaged Drinking Water. 
(c) Ministry of Health arid Fa mily Welfare is the enforcement/ 
implementing authority under the Prevention of Food Adulteration 
Rules. Bureau of Indian Standards is the certifying agency for Bottled 
Water. 
Quality control on mineral water manufacturing units 
3625. SHRI SANTOSH BAGROD IA: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether cancellation of license of the mineral water manufacturing 
units after detection of pesticides in bottled mineral water is the only 
logical action; 
(b) if not, what other action Government intend to take against such 
companies; 
(c) whether these companies are running several bottling plants in other 
parts of the country also; and 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
(d) if so, whether Government propose to check quality of water from their 
other units as well? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. 
SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) and (b) No BIS licence has been cancelled so 
far due to the presence of pesticide residues in bottled water. Only Stop 
Marking was imposed on some manufacturers of Packaged Drinking 
Water/Natural Mineral Water after observing deviations from the 
specifications prescribed in the relevant Indian Standards. Stop Marking 
instructions are issued in case of unsatisfactory performance/failure of 
samples. The stop marking does not m ean the cancellation of the licence. 
Under the stop marking, the manufacturer is not allowed to put the BIS mark 
on their product till the corrective actions are taken by the manufacturers 
which are duly verified by the Bureau of Indian Standards. 
(c) and (d) Some manufacturers may have more than one manufacturing 
plant in other parts of the country. Each such plant constitutes a separate 
licensee. Monitoring of performance of individual licence is done separately as 
per the Scheme of Testing and Inspection irrespective of the performance of its 
sister units operating in other parts of the country. 
Functioning of Consumer Fora 
3626.  SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER  AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of  the fact that the National 
Consumer Forum and the fora in the States are not functioning efficiently due to 
the lack of facilities including ministerial staff; 
(b) how many cases have been filed and disposed of by both the 
National and States Consumer Fora during the last three years; and 
(c) what facilities are planned to be provided to make them efficient and 
what budgetary support would be required for the purpose? 
124 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. 
SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) to (c) According to the provisions of the 
Consumer Protections Act, 1986, the responsibility for setting up of the 
Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions in the States and UTs and their 
effective functioning rests with  the State Governments and UT 
Administrations. However, to strengthe n the infrastructure for effective 
functioning of the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions in the 
States and UTs, Central Government has provided a one time financial 
assistance of Rs. 50 lakhs per State Commission and Rs. 10 lakhs per District 
Forum during 1995-99. Similarly, the responsibiility of setting up of the 
National Commission and its effective functioning rests with the Central 
Government. Necessary infrastructure including supporting staff and funds 
have been provided to the National Consumer Disputes Redressal 
Commission for its effective functioning. 
As per the information made available by the National Commission, 19, 
91, 131 cases have been filed before the consumer disputes redressal 
agencies, set up under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, out of which 
16,50,919 cases (82.9%) have already been disposed of by them since their 
inception, which is a considerable achievement by any standard.

Projects in Bhutan funded by India 
3635. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the mega projects in Bhutan which are being funded by 
Government along with the expenditure incurred on each project; and 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
(b) by when, these projects are likely to be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) and (b) At present there are three 
mega-projects under implementation in Bhutan which are funded by GOI. 
1020 MWTala Hydro-electric Project:  This Project is scheduled for 
commissioning by September 2005. The approved cost of the Project is Rs. 3580 
crores and is being funded on part Grant and part Loan basis. The loan is 
repayable in 12 equated annual instalment s and carries an interest rate of 9% 
per annum. Repayment of principle and interest would become due upon 
commencement of commercial operation of the project. Almost all the electricity 
generated by the project will be exported to India through the Eastern Grid. The 
Project is progressing as per schedule. 
Dungsum Cement Plant Project: The Project has two components: (i) The 
Dungsum Cement Plant at an approved cost of Rs . 300 crores and (ii) 
Associated Infrastructure at an approved cost of Rs. 100 crores. This is funded 
entirely by Government of India. Although the work on the main Cement 
Plant has been suspended due to prevailing difficult law and order situation in 
Eastern Bhutan, the work on related infrastructure is continuing. The 
infrastructure related work includes construction of Geleph-Tintibi-Nanglam 
transmission line (completed), constructiion of road from Pathsala (Assam) to 
Nangalam (Bhutan) and a Railway siding for the Cement Plant. 
60 MW Kurichu Project:  This Project has been recently 
commissioned. It was funded by Government of India on part Grant and part 
Loan basis at a total cost of Rs. 560 crores. The loan component is repayable in 24 
equated half yearly instalments and carries an interest rate of 10.75% per annum. 
The first repayment would commence from the date of full evacuation of power 
from Kurichu Project.

Health 
Assistance is being provided for the rehabilitation of Indira Gandhi 
Institute of Child Health (IGICH). 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003]

Demarcation of Indo-Bangla border 
3661. SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that still portions of the Indo-Bangla border 
remains undemarcated; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reasons or factors behind the inability to demarcate the same; 
(d) the consequence as a result thereof; 
(e) whether Government have taken up the matter with their 
Bangladesh counterparts; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) Yes. 
(b) A stretch of 6.1 Kms. of Indo-Bangladesh boundary is yet to be 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
(b) A stretch of 6.1 Kms. of Indo-Bangladesh boundary is yet to be 
demarcated in three segments. The thr ee segments are Daikhata-56 in West 
Bangal, Muhuri River (Belonia) in Tripura and Latitilla-Dumbari in Assam. 
(c) The demarcation is pending on account of difference of opinion over 
interpretation of the relevant articles of the Land Boundary Agreement of 
1974. 
(d) This has led to delay in the implementation of the 1974 Land 
Boundary Agreement. 
(e) Yes. 
(f) Following discussions at the diplomatic level, the Governments of 
India and Bangladesh have set up a Joint Boundary Working Group to address 
all issues relating to pending demarcation of the Indo-Bangladesh boundary. 
The Joint Boundary Working Group has held two meetings to far. 
Pressure on North Korea to dismantle atomic weapons 
3662. SHRI ARJUN SINGH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether he has urged the US that they should build pressure on North 
Korea instead of dealing with Iraq alone; 
(b) if so, whether Government are aware that the US Government is 
considering to pressurise China on North Korea; 
(c) whether both the countries, US and China, have been able to 
persuade North Korea to dismantle its atomic weapons; and 
(d) if so, to what extent? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (d)The North Korean question has 
been raised by India with its interlocutors at several levels. 
While responding to a question on the three-way meeting to be held in Beijing 
on North Korean issue, US Secretary of State Colic Powell stated on 16 April, in 
the course of a Press Interview in Washington DC, that "we have been in intence 
consultations with our friends in the region and we have put in place 
arrangements for a multilateral meeting, initially consisting 
172 

[24 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
of the United States, North Korea and Ch ina." Secretary of State Powell also 
stated that "This is good news for the region. It is good news for North 
Korea, frankly, because it gives them  the oppurtunity to present their 
positions, to come into this trilateral meeting and speak candidly in front of 
the United States and the Chinese with respect to their concerns; and it gives 
us the opportunity to do the same; and it gives the Chinese, who have a 
commitment to a non-nuclear Korean Pe ninsula, to express their point of 
view as well". 
Expenditure by Indian Missions and Posts 
3663. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that Rs. 756 crores in foreign exchange is being 
spent annually on our 156 Missions and Posts abroad; 
(b) whether some austerity measures ar e being introduced and if so, the 
percentage of savings anticipated thereby; 
(c) whether any study has been conducted towards relocation of some of 
the Indian Missions to make them cost effective; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) Yes. 
(b) In accordance with Ministry of Finance guidelines, austerity 
meassures such as cut of 25% in DA rates for local tours by officials in 
Missions/Posts abroad and ban on purchase of new vehicles has been 
introduced. The effect of austerity measures is offset by increasing 
cost of living at stations abroad as well as on account of depreciation 
of Indian currency vis-a-vis major currencies of the world. 
(c) and (d) The Ministry of reviews, on a regular basis, relocation of 
Indian Missions keeping in view the considerations of promotion of national 
interests in strategic, political, economic, commercial, consular and other 
spheres. In order to make our diplom atic representation cost effective, 
Ministry regularly looks at the possi bility of covering countries through 
Concurrent Accreditation. Presently, India has disptomatic relations with 81 
countries through Concurrent Accreditation.The Ministry also closed down 
14 Missions during the last 12 years with a view to cutting down on 
expenditure. 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
The Ministry has also been activel y pursuing a policy of purchase/ 
construction of properties abroad with a view to curtail expenditure on hiring 
of accommodation for Chancery and residences of India-based officers and 
staff members.

2003.

VIJAY GOEL): (a) The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 provides for different

consumption expenditure as the criterion to determine the persons living below 
the poverty line.The per-capita consumption norms has been fixed at Rs. 49.09 
per month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in urban areas at 1973-74 
prices at national level corresponding to a basket of goods and services 
anchored on a norm of per-capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in 
rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas.The states have different poverty lines, 
which are derived from the national level poverty lines, using state-specific 
price indices and inter-state price 
197

differentials. The national poverty line at 1999-2000 prices is Rs. 327.56 per-
capita per month in rural areas and Rs. 454.11 per-capita per month in urban 
areas. The poverty line for Uttar Prades h is 336.88 per-capita per month in 
ruraJ areas and Rs. 416.29 per capita per month in urban areas, at 1999-2000 
prices. 
There is no universally accepted definition of poverty line. However 
World Bank estimates percentage of persons living below a dollar a day at 
constant PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) for all the countries. 
(c) There is a three-pronged  action to alleviate and reduce poverty in the 
country. These are: (i) acceleration of economic growth, (ii) human, and social 
development through literacy, education, health, nutrition, meeting of the 
minimum needs, elevation of social and economic status of the weaker sections 
of the society, etc., and (iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and 
income generating programmes and assets-building for the poor.

Status of SSIs 
3709. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister ot SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the status of the small scale industries in different parts of the 
country in terms of implementation of the schemes under his Ministry; 
(b) the efforts made by his Ministry to encourage the small and medium 
industries; and 
(c) the growth in the small scale industries during the past five years, 
State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) to (c) Promotion and 
development of small scale industries is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments and Union Territories. The Central Government 
supplements the efforts of the State/UT Governments through various 
schemes/programmes relating to enhanced fiscal and credit support, better 
infrastructure, marketing facilities and incentives for technology upgradation. 
The Schmes/Programmes for the benefit of SSI sector are implemented 
uniformly throughout the country. Some of them are as under:— 
(1) Tool Rooms provide training facilities in the field of tool design, dye 
making, etc. 
(2) Central Footwear Training Institutes impart training on siroe 
design and related matters through CAD/CAM. 
(3) Process-cum-Product Development Centres provide training and 
undertake product development. 
(4) National institutes at three places impart training in the field of 
Entrepreneurial/Managerial Development Programmes. 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2003] 
(5) Under Integrated Infrastructural Development Schemes 62 
projects are at various stages of implementation. 
(6) Under Integrated Technology Upgradation and Management 
Programme, clusters of small scale industries are taken up for 
technology upgradation and other over all development. 
(7) ISO-9000/14001 Certification Reimbursement Scheme provides 
reimbursement upto Rs. 75,000/- or 75% of the cost, whichever is 
more incurred by the units for obtaining requisite certification 
from the competent authority. 
(8) Regional Testing Centres and Field Testing Stations provide 
testing facilities for BIS Standard of products. 
(9) The Marketing Development Assistance Scheme has been 
launched to introduce appropriate packaging and bar-coding of 
products. 
 
(10) Credit Guarantee Trust Fund has been set up to provide guarantee 
for collateral free credit facilities upto Rs. 25 lakh. 
(11) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme launched to provide 12% 
of capital subsidy for upgradation of technology. 
As a result of these efforts, the small scale sector accounts for 39% of 
industrial production, 34% in exports and has shown 4% growth rate in 
employment during the last decade in co mparison to 0.5% in the organized 
sector. The estimated number of SSI units increased from 29.44 lakh 
(registered and unregistered) in 1997-98 to 34.42 lakh in 2001 -02. The 
production of small scale units has increased from Rs. 411858 crore in 1996-
97 to Rs. 690316 crore in 2001-02 in monetary terms. Similarly, employment 
in SSI sector increased from

Launching of satellites 
3710.    MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the achievements of the ISRO in launching satellites, successfully 
testing of launch vehicles the new initia tives in space applications during the 
year 2002; and 
(b) whether these satellites can forecas t natural calamities such as 
cyclones, earthquakes, cloud bursts and the like? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRI SATYABRATA) MOOKHERJEE (a) The major achievements of ISRO 
during 2002 are: 
Launch and operationalisation of IN SAT-3C satellite in January, 2002 
augmenting the communication, broadcas ting and information infrastructure 
of the country. 
Launch and operationalisation of de dicated meteorological satellite 
KALPANA-1 (METSAT) onboard India's Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle in 
September, 2002 towards improved data for weather forecasting. 
Testing of indigenously developed cryogenic engine for the full flight 
duration. Initiatives in Space application including Tele-medicine - linking 
hospitals in the remote areas with the super specialty hospitals via INSAT 
satellites - and ground water prospect map preparation using satellite imagery 
to identify potential drinking water zones and ground water recharge 
structures. 
(b) The data from meteorological satellite such as KALPANA are used 
operationally by India Meteorological Department for monitoring 
225

and forecast of severe weather events  including cyclones, cloud bursts and 
heavy rainfall. Forecasting earthquakes is still a subject of research globally 
and satellite data provides important inputs towards such studies. 
Manned Lunar landing project 
3711.    SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: 
SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal for a manned lunar landing project; 
(b) if so, its aims, objectives and the cost; 
(c) the time frame for such a project; and 
(d) the funds alotted for the project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) There is no proposal at 
present for a manned lunar landing mission. However, the National Task 
Team set up to study a proposal for an unmanned orbiting spacecraft mission 
to moon has submitted its report. The proposal is to send an unmanned 
spacecraft to orbit the moon at a hei ght of 100 km. The spacecraft will be 
launched using India's own launch vehicle. The mission is planned for the 
scientific objective of high-resolution remote sensing of the lunar surface in 
visible, near-infrared, low-energy X-ray and high-energy X-ray spectra. 
(c) and (d) The time frame and funds allocations will be known only after 
the total review of the mission and the project report is finalized for the 
unmanned orbiting spacecraft mission.

development for the country. Sir, lots of ambitious plans were declared and 
we must look into one important issue that while we in this transition time 
are moving from PSUs to private sector, the digital divide has been 
widened. There is disproportionate development, and if we allow this 
disproportionate development to carry on, we cannot unite the country. 
I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister that there 
were a large number of promises made by the Government in the past for 
bringing the land-locked North-Eastern Region closer to the main land 
through an effective communication netw ork. But the hard reality reveals a 
reverse trend, of depriving the region  from all the recent developments. I 
want to cite some examples. The International Internet Gateway 
commissioned by the BSNL with a second-hand outdated dish antenna was 
brought from Orissa to Guwahati, which could not operate even for a single 
day. The net fee call centre operati ng through the STPI gateway failed due 
to high cost of bandwidth. The only available Kolkata-Guwahati BSNL fibre 
network is also worst and unreliable requiring the highest down time. Total 
line Internet Service Providers operatin g in the region did nothing except 
siphoning out money to invest outside the region. In our country, a total 
number of 56 International Internet Ga teways are operating in India. An 
application for licence by local company for opening an international 
gateway at Guwahati took more than a year for its clearance, despite 
fulfilling all the required formalities for clearance.

*504. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA : Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a price control on imported 
formulations also; 
(b) what is Government's policy and which are the products that have been 
granted price approval of import of formulations; 
8 

[25 April, 2003] RAJYASABHA 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Ely Lilly, Nicholas, Aventis have flouted 
the DPCO fully in case of finished fo rmulations prices; if so, the details 
thereof; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that these cases have been referred to CBI 
for further probe? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SUKH 
DEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Prices of scheduled imported formulations are fixed as per 
para 7 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995, by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) . Para 7 provides that the landed 
cost shall form the basis for fixing its price alongwith such margin to cover 
selling and distribution expenses including interest and importer's profit which 
shall not exceed fifty per cent of the landed cost. Importers of non-Scheduled 
formulations fix their price on their own as per cost of import and prevailing 
market competition etc. NPPA regularly examines the movement in prices of 
non-scheduled formulations (including imported formulations) on the basis of 
information available to it from various sources. 
(c) and (d) No case of flouting Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
provisions/price violation in case of finished formulation prices has come to 
the notice of National Phar maceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in respect of 
M/s Ely Lilly, M/s Nicholas and M/s Aventis. However, a technical fault in the 
prices charged by M/s Aventis Pharma Limited for two imported Insulin 
formulations came to the notice of NPPA . This has not been referred to CBI 
for further probe.

Utilisation of funds given for Yamuna Action Plan 
*506. SHRIS. S. AHLUWALIA : Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the reports in the 
media highlighting continuous rise in the pollution level in the River Yamuna 
despite huge outlay of Rs. 600 crore incurred on the Yamuna Action Plan (YAP): 
(b) if so. Government's comments about the veracity of the report. 
(c) measures taken by Government to ensure judicious utilisation of the 
fund so received from the Japanese Government; and 
(d) the reasons for continuous deterioration of pollution and non 
availability of cleaner water in the river even after huge investment for this 
purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) Under the Yamuna Action Plan, Phase-I of Government 
which has been funded by the Japan Bank for International Co-operation a total 
expenditure of Rs. 668 crore has been incurred on pollution abatement works in 
Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh. Major works implemented under the plan 
are:— 
Sewerage —      170kms. 
Main Pumping Stations —     60 nos. 
Sewage treatment plants        —     32 nos. (734 mid) 
Community Toilets —     1123 nos. (out of which 960 toilet 
complexes have been constructed in 
Delhi) 
In addition, the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi has 
also taken up the work of construction of sewage treatment plants at 17 locations. 
Despite these works, the water quality of Yamuna has not shown appreciable 
improvement along Delhi due to the following reasons : 
(i) As against the present sewage generation of 3300 mid, the installed 
sewage treatment capacity is 2300 mid. Thus, there is a gap of 1000 
mid in the sewage treatment capacity. 
3 9 

RAJYA SABHA [25 April, 2003] 
(ii) Out of about 130 km. length of trunk sewer, about 90 km. length 
requires refurbishing and rehab ilitation as the sewers are either 
silted up or settled. As a result, the installed capacity of sewage 
treatment plant is not fully utili zed and the untreated sewage is 
discharged in the river through various drains. 
(iii) Out of a total of  15 common effluent treatment plants to be 
constructed in 21 industrial estates, only 3 have been completed so 
far. The remaining ones are targeted for completion by December, 
2003. 
(iv) Lack of dilution capacity in the river particularly along Delhi. 
Some of the major works of construction of additional sewage treatment 
plants and refurbishing and rehabilitation of trunk sewers have been included 
in the Yamuna Action Plan Phase-II. In addition, the National Capital Territory 
of Delhi has also taken up the work of construction of two large Sewage 
Treatment Plants. All the riparian states of Yamuna except Delhi have also 
agreed to release their share in the minimum flow of fresh water of 10 cubic 
metres per second along the Delhi stretch of the river. Government of National 
Capital Territory of Delhi has expressed its inability lo release its share of 
minimum flow which is 4.6%. due to shortage of drinking water in Delhi. 
The implementation of river cleaning programme is reviewed by both the 
Govt, oflndia and the State Govt, at various levels regularly. Funds are released 
to the Implementing Agencies of the St ate Governments only after the receipt 
of proper utilization certificates authenticated by competent authorities.

Conversion of waste plastic into fuels 
*519. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Nagpur based Scientist has successfully 
invented a unique process converting waste plastic into fuels: 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) whether this invented fuel is environment friendly? 
THE MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) As per the informa tion available. Professor Alka Umesh 
Zadgaonkar. Head of the Department of Applied Chemistry in GH Raisoni College 
of Engineering, Nagpur has worked out a process for conversion of waste plastic 
into fuels. The salient process features include : 
• Feeding of shredded plastic waste into a reactor. 
• When the shredded plastic is heat ed at 350 degree centigrade in 
the presence of a catalyst it forms a mixed fuel. 
• In the second stage when the mixed fuel is subjected to fractional 
distillation it forms petrol (50%) kerosene (20%) diesel (25%) and 
lubricating oil (5%). 
The liquid fuel obtained from this process is stated to contain insignificant 
concentrations of sulphur and nitrogen, which is comparable with natural gasoline 
in its quality parameters.

SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether according to C AG report number 5 of 2002,1 ARI's objective of 
Centre for Academic Excellence could not be achieved in full despite the fact

of students admitted for different courses;

been included in the CAG Report No. 5 of 2002. The Action Taken Notes (ATN) 
to this para were furnished to the Principal Director of Audit (Scientific 
Department), New Delhi forgetting on 6.8.2002. However, Indian Agricultural 
Research Institute (IARI) achieved its  objective as a Centre of Academic

Policy for rain fed fanning 
3723. MS. PRAMILA BOHTDAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have formulated a comprehensive policy for rainfed farming 
in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the time by which such a policy would be in place ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV) : (a) Government of India have formulated a 
comprehensive National Agriculture Policy in July, 2000. It includes policy for rainfed 
farming in the country. 
(b) The National Agriculture Policy, 2000. as it pertains to rainfed farming, 
provides : 
• Integrated and holistic development of rainfed areas will be promoted by 
conservation of rain water by vegetative measures on watershed basis and 
augmentation of biomass production through agro and farm forestry with the 
involvement of the watershed community. 
• All spatial components of a watershed, /. e. arable land, non-arable and drainage 
lines will be treated as one geo-hydrological entity. 
• Management of grazing land will receive greater attention for augmenting 
availability of animal feed and fodder.

Decaying Mahabodhi tree 
3781. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : W ill the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government's attention has been drawn to the news that 
appeared in media regarding Mahabodhi tree facing pest threat; and 
(b) the curative measures Government propose to take to prevent further 
deterioration of tree? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI DHJP SINGH JUDEV): (a) and(b) Yes. Sir The following measures 
have been taken to protect the tree from the attack of pest and decay : 
(i) Removal of loose bark from the main trunk of the Bodhi Tree through sharp 
sickle/kharpi. 
(ii) Application of Boardeaux mixture (1 : 1 : 10) on the trunk and the 
branches through brush. 
(iii) Fortnightly spraying of the mixture of Vapone (1 millilitre/Utre of water) and 
Sandovit (1/2 millilitre/litre of water) for pest control and Multiplex to supplement 
the nutrients. 
(iv) Removal of weeds from the adjacent lawns situated on the western side of 
the Bodhi Tree. 
(v) The pulverization of the soil of the lawn with the help of spade and 
application of 2 kg. of Potassium Sulphate, 5kg. of Single Superphosphate and 30 kg. 
of Neem cake. 
(vi) Gradual pruning of excess growth of branches on annual basis in the 
presence of a Horticulture Expert and painting of the cut portion with Bordeaux paste. 
(vii) Providing sufficient irrigation through pits dug in the lawns adjacent to the 
Bodhi Tree. 
(viii) Regular monitoring through the Bodh Gaya Temple Management 
Committee under the Chairmanship of the District Magistrate, Gaya.

Education to children 
3795. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI:   Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state : 
(a) whether 3 crores 20 lacs children in  the age group of 6 years to 10 
years are not going to school; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what measures are being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) and (b) Out of a child 
population of 11.83 crore in the age-group 6-11 years projected by the 
Registrar General of India for the year 2001, 11.38 crore children were enrolled 
in schools as on 30th Sept. 2000, as reported in the Selected Educational 
Statistics 2000-2001 brought out by this Ministry. The reasons for non-
enrolment of school children include habitations not having facilities for 
education, socio-economic factors preventing children from going to schools 
and children dropping out of school after getting enrolled. 
(c) The Government has taken a number of steps to ensure 
Universalisation of Elementary Education. The Constitution (86th 
Amendment) Act, 2002 to make elem entary education a Fundamental Right 
has been enacted. The Government has also launched the scheme of Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan as a National Programme to achieve the goal of 
Universalisation of Elementary Education in a Mission mode in partnership 
with States. This programme focuses, in  particular, on the educational needs 
of girls, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, Minorities, urban deprived 
children and other children in difficult circumstances.
